papers.title: A superconducting qutrit link beyond the qubit limit
papers.abstract: Superconducting microwave links have enabled deterministic state transfer and remote entanglement between qubits, but deterministic links have so far operated with an effectively two-dimensional transmitted Hilbert space. Here we demonstrate a superconducting qutrit link between two independently packaged nodes connected by a microwave channel. Each node combines a transmon qutrit, a transmission resonator, and a tunable Purcell-filter interface, allowing the two remote microwave-photon interfaces to be matched in both frequency and bandwidth. We implement two transition-selective photon-mediated operations that transfer the $|e\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ qutrit components in distinct temporal modes of the same channel. We tomographically characterize arbitrary qutrit-state transfer, obtaining a mean transferred-state fidelity of 83.68% and a qutrit process fidelity of 77.12%, exceeding both the classical qutrit-transfer benchmark and the best possible average fidelity of an effective qubit channel used to transmit an arbitrary qutrit. Using partial-transfer operations, we reconstruct a remote two-qutrit state with negativity 0.730, a tomography-inferred dense-coding capacity of 2.273 bits, and a tomography-inferred Collins-Gisin-Linden-Massar-Popescu (CGLMP) parameter $I_3=2.332$, all beyond the corresponding qubit or local bounds. These results demonstrate a superconducting microwave link that uses the native three-level structure of transmons as a genuine high-dimensional communication resource.

Transmon qubit readout fidelity at the threshold for quantum error correction without a quantum-limited amplifier

summary.summary: This work demonstrates a superconducting microwave link between two independently packaged transmon qutrit nodes, achieving arbitrary qutrit-state transfer with 83.68% mean fidelity and 77.12% process fidelity, and generating remote entanglement with negativity 0.730 and tomography-inferred dense-coding capacity 2.273 bits. The protocol uses transition-selective photon-mediated operations ($e0g1$ sideband and $f0g1$ cavity-assisted Raman) to transfer the $|e\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ amplitudes in distinct temporal modes through a tunable Purcell-filtered interface matched at 7.4347 GHz.
summary.motivation: While superconducting microwave links have enabled deterministic state transfer between qubits, extending this to genuine three-level communication requires mapping the full qutrit Hilbert space onto the traveling field without simultaneously opening all transitions to the continuum. This work tests whether the native three-level structure of transmons can serve as a high-dimensional resource beyond effective qubits.
summary.method: Two transmon qutrits in separate sample boxes are connected by a one-metre cascaded microwave channel. Each node contains an auxiliary transmission resonator and tunable Purcell filter that allow frequency and bandwidth matching between remote interfaces. Two chirped 200 ns sine-envelope pulses implement transition-selective photon-mediated primitives: $e0g1$ couples $|e,0\rangle \leftrightarrow |g,1\rangle$ via flux-parametric sideband, while $f0g1$ couples $|f,0\rangle \leftrightarrow |g,1\rangle$ via cavity-assisted Raman. Full qutrit transfer applies both primitives sequentially; partial transfers generate remote two-qutrit entanglement.
summary.result: Qutrit state transfer exceeds both the classical measure-and-prepare limit (1/2) and the maximum average fidelity 3/4 for transmitting an arbitrary qutrit through a qubit channel. Remote entanglement fidelity 81.21% exceeds the Schmidt-rank-two bound 2/3, negativity 0.730 exceeds the two-qubit maximum 0.5, dense-coding capacity 2.273 bits exceeds the qubit limit 2 bits, and CGLMP parameter $I_3=2.332$ exceeds the local bound 2.

papers.title: Voltage-tunable Josephson Junctions on Germanium Quantum Wells with in-situ Aluminum Contacts
papers.abstract: Voltage-tunable Josephson junctions (VT-JJs) are an emerging element in superconducting quantum electronics with potential to expand the functionality of conventional designs. While VT-JJs are largely compatible with wafer-scale semiconductor processing, their integration into quantum circuits remains a challenge due to unmitigated semiconductor microwave loss. Here, a deep mesa etch process, wherein the epitaxial material is removed except the VT-JJ device, will facilitate the integration of VT-JJs with low-microwave-loss circuit elements by allowing these circuit elements to be placed directly on a low-loss substrate. A Germanium quantum well is grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) on a float zone silicon substrate with in-situ deposited aluminum contacts. This combination allows the formation of an oxide-free superconductor-semiconductor interface. The deep mesa etch process is optimized to produce a sidewall taper sufficient for continuous metal deposition from the substrate to the top of the mesa for electrostatic gate electrodes and interconnects. The fabricated Josephson junctions demonstrate gate-tunable supercurrents with a maximum critical current over 100 nA and critical-current normal-resistance product of $8.63~μV$. These results demonstrate a pathway toward improved integration of voltage-tunable superconducting circuit elements with quantum electronic building blocks such as couplers and qubits.

similar_to.title: Electrical post-fabrication tuning of aluminum Josephson junctions at room temperature

summary.summary: Voltage-tunable Josephson junctions are fabricated on MBE-grown shallow Ge quantum wells (16 nm) with in-situ Al contacts on float-zone Si substrates using a deep mesa etch process that enables monolithic integration with low-loss superconducting circuits. The devices demonstrate gate-tunable supercurrents reaching 103 nA at $V_g = -17.5$ V with an $I_C R_N$ product of 8.63 µV and extracted interface transparency of 4–9%.
summary.motivation: Integration of voltage-tunable JJs into highly coherent quantum circuits requires wafer-scale platforms with low microwave loss and oxide-free superconductor-semiconductor interfaces to eliminate flux noise from tuning.
summary.method: A deep mesa etch ($\sim$2.6 µm tall with 18° sidewall taper) was optimized to remove lossy epitaxial buffer except at the junction, allowing continuous metal deposition from the low-loss Si substrate to gate electrodes; transport characterized at 10 mK shows gate-tunable supercurrent via Hall bars indicating peak mobility of 26,800 cm$^2$/Vs and mean free path of 482 nm.
summary.result: Maximum critical current of 103 nA with $I_C R_N = 8.63$ µV enables transmon tuning between 4.25 and 8.7 GHz ($E_J/E_C$ from 62 to 348) for typical design values; STEM confirms abrupt Al/Ge interfaces without chemical intermixing and no residual processing damage.

papers.title: Repetition-code-based readout error detection and correction across hardware platforms and generations
papers.abstract: Readout errors are one of the dominant sources of noise in current quantum processors, limiting both expectation-value estimation and sampling-based applications. Since they affect only the classical measurement outcomes, they can be addressed using classical coding techniques: immediately before measurement, each data qubit is redundantly encoded with ancilla qubits, and the resulting bit string is decoded either by post-selection or by majority voting. Unlike conventional readout error mitigation, which corrects only aggregate quantities such as expectation values, this approach operates on individual measurement shots and can therefore produce approximately corrected samples. We present a systematic cross-platform and cross-generation experimental evaluation of repetition-code readout error detection and correction. We benchmark the same protocol on IBM Heron r1-r3 superconducting processors and Quantinuum H1 and H2 trapped-ion processors while independently varying the code distance, hardware generation, and encoding layout. We find that both error detection and correction improve readout fidelity on every device and generation tested, even as the unencoded baseline improves substantially across successive hardware releases. At the same time, the value of additional redundancy depends strongly on the underlying hardware. On superconducting processors, the extra gate errors introduced by the encoding rapidly offset its benefits, whereas on trapped-ion processors the much lower gate error rates allow larger code distances to remain advantageous.

similar_to.title: Benchmarking the readout of a superconducting qubit for repeated measurements
Realizing Repeated Quantum Error Correction in a Distance-Three Surface Code

summary.summary: This work benchmarks repetition-code-based readout error detection and correction across IBM Heron r1–r3 superconducting processors and Quantinuum H1–H2 trapped-ion devices, varying code distance, hardware generation, and encoding layout. Both error detection (unanimous-vote decoding with post-selection) and correction (majority-vote decoding) improve readout fidelity on every device tested, but the benefit of larger code distances depends strongly on the underlying hardware: on superconducting processors, encoding gate errors offset gains rapidly, whereas trapped-ion devices' lower two-qubit gate error rates allow larger codes to remain advantageous.
summary.motivation: Readout errors dominate noise in current quantum processors and limit sampling-based applications, but unlike conventional mitigation schemes that correct only aggregate statistics, shot-by-shot readout error mitigation could yield individually corrected samples. The relative performance of repetition-code methods across qualitatively different hardware platforms and successive hardware generations remained unexplored.
summary.method: The authors implemented $[n,1]$ repetition-code encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors using $n-1$ CNOT gates in star or chain layouts, then compared unencoded baselines against unanimous-vote decoding (post-selecting shots where data and ancilla qubits agree) and majority-vote decoding (correcting every shot) while varying code distance and input state.
summary.result: Error detection improved readout fidelity on all devices; for random/all-ones inputs on superconducting devices, benefit saturated at $[2,1]$ due to gate error accumulation, while on trapped-ion devices $[3,1]$ codes provided further gains. Post-selection retention fell to ~4% for $[4,1]$ on 24 qubits (IBM Pittsburgh) versus >90% on Quantinuum H1-1 (6 qubits). Majority-vote correction on the chain layout degraded fidelity on superconducting hardware but improved it on trapped-ion devices.

papers.title: Untangling QLDPC Codes with Biased Noise Ancilla
papers.abstract: Remarkable technical progress has made high-rate, high-distance, quantum low-density parity-check codes (QLDPC) promising candidates for scalable quantum computing. However, it is hard to design low-depth syndrome extraction circuits that do not spread errors from ancilla qubits to multiple data qubits, also known as hook errors, for general QLDPC codes. Additionally, widely used decoders for these codes based on belief propagation are impaired due to short loops in the Tanner graph. Here, we investigate a hardware-aware approach to avoid these hooks and loops using biased noise ancillas. Using examples of bicycle bivariate codes and a cyclic hypergraph product code, which have been widely considered for practical application, we show that the effective fault-distance of the conventional syndrome extraction circuit can be significantly higher and the number of short loops can be significantly lower when the ancillas are subject to phase-flip errors only, compared to when they are also subject to bit-flip errors. This can result in almost an order of magnitude improvement in the logical error rate at circuit noise of $2\times 10^{-3}$ and when bit-flip errors in the ancilla are 50 times less likely than phase-flip errors. Our work demonstrates a significant and practical quantum error correction advantage with biased noise qubits in which full-bias cannot be maintained.

similar_to.title: Quantum error correction at ultra-low overhead

summary.summary: This work demonstrates that restricting noise bias to ancilla qubits in syndrome extraction circuits can significantly improve the performance of quantum low-density parity-check codes without requiring code tailoring or bias-preserving CX gates. For the [[144,12,12]] bicycle bivariate code at circuit noise $p = 2 	imes 10^{-3}$ with ancilla bit-flip suppression $	imes 50$, ancilla-only biased noise achieves an 8.5-fold reduction in logical error rate compared to depolarizing noise, primarily through elimination of hook errors and reduction of short cycles in the Tanner graph.
summary.motivation: Standard syndrome extraction for QLDPC codes suffers from hook errors (ancilla faults propagating to multiple data qubits) that reduce circuit-level distance and from short loops in the Tanner graph that impair belief propagation decoding. Previous biased-noise QEC schemes required difficult-to-implement bias-preserving CX gates or code redesign.
summary.method: We simulated circuit-level memory storage using three instances of bicycle bivariate codes ([[72,12,6]], [[90,8,10]], [[144,12,12]]) and the [[336,20,6]] cyclic hypergraph product code under four noise models: depolarizing, ancilla-only biased ($	ext{BIAS}_2[	au, p]$ on ancilla-controlled gates), non-CX biased (CZ-preserving bias without bias-preserving CX), and full-bias (Z-errors only). We quantified hook errors via circuit-level distance bounds and counted 4- and 6-cycles in detector error model Tanner graphs, then compared logical error rates using BP+OSD-CS-7 decoding with joint X-Z syndrome decoding.
summary.result: At $	au = 100$ and $p = 2 	imes 10^{-3}$, the [[144,12,12]] code with ancilla-only biased noise achieved 8.5-fold logical error rate reduction versus depolarizing noise; the [[336,20,6]] HGP code achieved 4.2-fold reduction. Circuit-level distance was restored from 10 to 12 for the [[90,8,10]] code under biased ancilla. Short 4-cycles and 6-cycles were reduced by orders of magnitude: for the gross code, 4-cycles dropped from 12.5M (depolarizing) to 1.2M (ancilla-only bias) to 79k (full-bias).

papers.title: Dissipative Effects in Transmission Line Analogues of Hawking Radiation
papers.abstract: Hawking radiation is a fundamental result of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, yet its direct observation remains beyond current experimental capabilities. Circuit quantum electrodynamics provides a practical platform for realizing analogue systems where Hawking-like radiation may be studied under controlled laboratory conditions. In this work, we analyze two superconducting-circuit analogues of Schwarzschild black holes: a tunable dc-SQUID transmission line and a SNAIL-based transmission line supporting solitonic solutions of the KdV equation. We investigate the conditions under which these architectures can generate an observable Hawking temperature and study the impact of dissipation and thermal noise using an open quantum systems approach. To assess the observability of the Hawking signal, we propose complementing particle number measurements with estimates of the Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the thermal bath. Our analysis establishes practical detectability thresholds and shows that Hawking temperatures above approximately 73 mK remain distinguishable under realistic experimental conditions. While the tunable transmission line architecture can reach temperatures of about 113 mK and therefore appears more viable, the solitonic model requires further optimization and more demanding experimental conditions.

similar_to.title: On-demand driven dissipation for cavity reset and cooling

summary.summary: This paper analyzes dissipative effects in two superconducting-circuit analogues of Schwarzschild black holes that generate Hawking radiation: a tunable dc-SQUID transmission line and a SNAIL-based transmission line supporting solitonic KdV solutions. Using open quantum systems theory, the authors establish detectability thresholds and show that Hawking temperatures above approximately 73 mK remain distinguishable from thermal backgrounds under realistic experimental conditions.
summary.motivation: Direct observation of Hawking radiation from astrophysical black holes is impossible due to vanishingly small temperatures. Circuit QED provides a practical platform to study analogue Hawking radiation, but environmental coupling, dissipation, and thermal noise may obscure the quantum signal, requiring quantitative analysis of experimental feasibility.
summary.method: The authors modeled dissipation using the Lindblad equation with relaxation rates and dephasing typical of superconducting qubits ($\tau_\kappa = 100$ µs, $\tau_\gamma = 20$ µs). They computed the Hilbert-Schmidt distance between the evolved Hawking state and the thermal bath to establish a distinguishability threshold ($D = 0.05$) over measurement timescales of $2$ µs.
summary.result: The tunable transmission line architecture achieves a Hawking temperature of 113 mK, which exceeds the experimental threshold of 73 mK and remains observable. The solitonic KdV analogue reaches only 1.9 mK, falling far below detectability thresholds even under optimistic conditions with $\tau_\kappa = 200$ µs and bath temperature of 10 mK.
